idiom_name: tower Layer/Service or axum middleware::from_fn wrapping the router
implementation_notes: The default realization: implement the check as a tower Service/Layer (configurable, shareable as a crate) or, for application-local guards, as an async fn used with middleware::from_fn. It wraps a whole router or route group, so the rule is declared once for many endpoints and runs before any extractor or handler logic. Use Router::route_layer for guarded groups and Router::layer for global concerns, and remember that axum's onion model means the last applied layer sees the request first.
pitfalls: Layer order is the policy: .layer() only wraps routes added before it and route_layer skips unmatched routes, so a router assembled in the wrong order leaves paths unguarded.
Holding a borrow of the request across an await point forces a clone or fails to compile; extract owned identity data (Arc<Principal>) before calling the decision.
Middleware whose error type is converted to Ok keeps calling the inner service, turning a denial into normal processing.

variants.name: Extractor guard (FromRequestParts with a rejecting type)
variants.implementation_notes: The type-driven realization: encode the permission requirement in a marker type implementing FromRequestParts<S> whose Rejection is a 403 (or a redirect), so a handler that names the extractor cannot compile without the check and a denial never reaches the handler body. axum documents this with middleware::from_extractor when the same type is wanted both as an extractor and as a middleware, and its example is literally an extractor that performs authorization. Prefer it when the guard is per handler and should be visible in the signature; prefer the layer when many routes share one rule.
pitfalls: A handler that omits the extractor parameter is simply unguarded, so reserve this form for routes that are meant to be individually annotated and keep a global layer as the floor.
The rejection must be an HTTP response (IntoResponse): returning an internal error type without conversion produces a 500 instead of a 403.
Extractors run in argument order, so a body-consuming extractor placed before the guard lets a denied request stream a payload before the decision.
